title: Agent loops die silently when .goose-task.md is deleted by a rebase onto main
description: ROOT CAUSE CONFIRMED BY TIMELINE. Untracking .goose-task.md (necessary - it held a sudo password, ob-3i5) means any device node that merges or rebases onto main has the file DELETED from its working tree. goose-loop.sh passes it unconditionally as 'goose run -i $TASK' with no existence check, so goose fails every iteration while the loop keeps spinning on its 20s sleep and 'git commit' finds nothing to commit - no error surfaces anywhere except the untracked local log. Timeline: 03:12 UTC the file was untracked on the feature branch; 09:33 that landed on main via PR #9; 14:38 the j2 node rebased onto main; 14:38-14:48 j2 pushed 5 commits from its already-loaded session; 14:48 last commit, then silence. j2 is the only node that has rebased onto main and it is the only node whose branch no longer tracks the file. FIX APPLIED: committed docs/agent-task.template.md (credential-free, placeholders __BRANCH__/__HOST__/__DEVICE__/__BINARY__/__RESULT_NAME__) and an ensure_task() self-heal in goose-loop.sh that regenerates the task from the template when missing, substituting per-node values from ORION_DEVICE/ORION_BINARY/ORION_RESULT_NAME env vars. Verified end-to-end with a stub goose: loop detects the missing file, logs '[self-heal: ... regenerating from template]', writes a 63-line task with zero unsubstituted placeholders, and invokes goose successfully. OPERATOR ACTION STILL NEEDED: the fix only helps once a node has the new goose-loop.sh, so each stalled node must be restarted by hand (git pull, set ORION_* in the shell profile, relaunch the tmux loop). Nodes j2 (2h44m idle), r5 (9h11m), t3 and t4 (15h25m) are all currently not producing work.

title: Run the device-fleet bandwidth-scaling study (Pi 5 / RK3588 / Jetson Nano)
description:
THE FIRST REAL MEASUREMENTS, and the strongest result available without the O6. See ADR 0005.

Run bench_gdn on all three devices at 30 repeats and collect CSV plus a manifest per device. Use the core-tuned binaries: bench_gdn_pi5_a76, bench_gdn_rk3588_a76 (taskset to the big cluster), bench_gdn_rk3588_a55 (little cluster), bench_gdn_jetson_a57.

The study, not the individual numbers, is the deliverable. The three devices span 17 / 25.6 / ~34 GB/s of spec bandwidth. If GDN decode is bandwidth-bound at ~0.25 FLOP/byte as METRICS.md argues, achieved throughput should track spec bandwidth roughly linearly and INDEPENDENTLY OF CORE GENERATION.

The discriminating case: the Pi 5 has the NEWEST cores (A76, Armv8.2, dotprod) but the LOWEST bandwidth (17 GB/s, 32-bit LPDDR4X), while the Jetson Nano has the OLDEST cores (A57, Armv8.0, no dotprod) and MORE bandwidth (25.6 GB/s, 64-bit LPDDR4). If the Nano beats the Pi 5 on the scan kernel despite three ISA generations less capability, that is strong evidence for bandwidth-boundedness rather than a confirmation-biased result.

Also: extrapolate to the O6's 100 GB/s and publish it as a PREDICTION, so it can be checked later if a board arrives. Predicting then confirming is far stronger than measuring once.

Verify achieved GiB/s against each device's spec sheet - the RK3588 figure is estimated from its quad-channel 16-bit interface and needs confirming on hardware. Do not close this bead without committed manifests (PLAN.md section 9).
close_reason: Fleet bandwidth-scaling study landed via the cherry-pick of bench/j2's analysis: results/figures/fleet_bandwidth_scaling.md plus bench/fleet_analysis.py as the regenerator, and FINDINGS 5b. The discriminating test from ADR 0005 is answered: the Pi 5 beats the Jetson on all three kernels despite 33% LESS spec bandwidth, so the pure bandwidth-bound thesis is INCOMPLETE at seq=64 - at 4096 channels the working set is ~1 MiB and L2/L3-resident, making it instruction-overhead-bound rather than DRAM-bound. Core microarchitecture dominates. Follow-on ob-bf7 covers the replicate-spread problem that prevents any quantitative slope; the O6 prediction ships as ~3-8 GiB/s rather than a fitted line.

title: Standalone GDN kernel microbenchmark for any aarch64 device (Armv8 upward)
description:
Bridges verified-correct to MEASURED. The maintainer has Armv8 devices available, which unblocks real Arm silicon numbers without the O6.

Build a dependency-free, statically-linked aarch64 binary that can be copied to any Armv8+ device and run to produce the project's first real performance numbers. Must: time all three GDN kernels (cumdecay, gated scan, causal dwconv1d) at Qwen3.5-4B shapes (2048 channels, chunk 64) and 0.8B shapes; report which dispatch path actually compiled in (SVE/NEON/scalar); follow docs/METRICS.md's statistical protocol (discarded warmups, N repeats, p50 and p95, never a single best run); emit CSV rows conforming to docs/RESULTS_SCHEMA.md; and derive achieved memory bandwidth so the bandwidth-bound thesis can be checked against the device's spec rather than asserted.

Armv8 caveats to respect and report rather than paper over: most Armv8 cores have NO SVE (so this measures the NEON path, which is the point), i8mm needs Armv8.6+, and dotprod needs Armv8.2+. The binary should report what it actually detected.
close_reason:
bench_gdn.c plus scripts/build_device_bench.sh. Dependency-free, statically-linked microbenchmark: one binary copies to any aarch64 device and runs with no toolchain, Python, or shared libs on target. Four ISA variants built (armv8a / armv8.2dot / armv8.6i8mm / armv9sve2). Times all three kernels at verified Qwen3.5-4B and 0.8B shapes, follows METRICS.md protocol (3 discarded warmups, p50/p95, refuses N<5), reports the dispatch path actually compiled in (verified: armv9sve2 reports sve, armv8a reports neon, so dispatch is real not collapsed), emits schema-conforming CSV, and derives achieved GiB/s from explicit traffic accounting so the bandwidth-bound thesis can be tested against device spec rather than assumed.

Documented loudly in docs/FINDINGS.md section 5 that QEMU timings are performance-MEANINGLESS (emulation artefacts, up to 97% spread) and must never appear in a result table - QEMU's role here is correctness only. No performance results are claimed yet; the apparatus is ready and awaits real silicon.

title: Author minimal per-operator ONNX probe graphs for the NOE op-coverage audit
description:
Prep work that makes ob-t3b.1 mechanical the moment the NOE SDK is in hand: emit one minimal ONNX graph per GDN constituent operator family so a cixbuild failure is attributable to exactly one operator.

Deliberately hand-authored with onnx.helper rather than exported from torch. The torch exporter fuses and decomposes ops unpredictably, so a rejected torch-exported graph would not tell us WHICH operator the compiler choked on - which is the entire point of the audit. Hand-building also avoids a ~300MB torch dependency for graphs that are a few KB each.

Probe families, mirroring Qwen3.5's verified GDN layer shapes (linear_conv_kernel_dim=4, linear_key/value_head_dim=128, linear_num_key_heads=16):
  1. causal depthwise Conv1D with left padding
  2. gated decay as Log -> CumSum -> Exp (ONNX has no CumProd op, so this decomposition is itself a coverage question)
  3. delta-rule state update (MatMul / outer product / Sub / Transpose)
  4. elementwise gate chains (Sigmoid / Softplus / Mul)
  5. ONNX Scan and Loop control flow - the chunkwise recurrence needs one of these, and NPU compilers frequently lack control-flow support. This is the most likely failure point and therefore the most valuable probe.

Done when the generator runs, every graph passes onnx.checker, and a README documents the exact cixbuild invocation to run against each once the SDK lands.
close_reason: scripts/npu_op_probe.py emits 6 minimal per-operator ONNX graphs into artifacts/npu_op_probe/ with a manifest. Hand-authored via onnx.helper rather than torch-exported so a cixbuild failure is attributable to exactly one operator. Verified known-good before use: all 6 pass onnx.checker full_check, all 6 execute under onnxruntime 1.28 with finite outputs, and the causal conv is verified genuinely causal (perturbing the last timestep leaves earlier outputs bit-identical). README documents the cixbuild invocation and how to record results, including the silent-CPU-fallback case which looks like success and performs like failure.

title: NOE op-coverage audit for GDN operators on an x86 host (no board required)
description:
Unblocked by the 2026-08-02 CIX finding (docs/CLAIM_VERIFICATION.md 2.2a): the NOE Compiler is a direct download with no approval gate, requires Python 3.10, and runs on an x86 Linux HOST rather than the board. So the highest-value early finding in the whole project is available today with no hardware.

Install the SDK in a miniforge Python 3.10 venv, verify with 'cixbuild -v', then attempt to compile the GDN constituent operators and record exactly what the compiler accepts, silently falls back on, or rejects: causal Conv1D, cumulative-product/decay gating, the delta-rule state update, and the elementwise gate chains. Export minimal ONNX graphs for each op rather than the whole model so failures are attributable to a single operator.

This directly addresses risk R3 and produces docs/FINDINGS.md content that is reusable by anyone porting a GDN-class model to this silicon. A negative result ('the NOE Compiler has no kernel for a gated recurrent scan') is the finding, not a failure - it is the empirical justification for routing the scan to GPU/CPU in the mapping ADR.

Only RUNNING the compiled artifact needs the board; compiling does not. Supersedes the hardware-gated framing of ob-8xc for the compile-time half of that audit.
notes: Dependency on ob-37v (arch audit) removed as over-specified: the probe graphs only needed the GDN layer SHAPES, which were already verified from primary sources in docs/CLAIM_VERIFICATION.md 2.3 (conv kernel 4, key/value head dim 128, 16 key heads). A full per-checkpoint architecture audit was not a prerequisite for operator coverage. ob-37v remains valuable for the mapping work but does not gate this.
close_reason: AUDIT COMPLETE on x86 host with no board. Headline: every arithmetic operator GDN needs is natively supported (CumSum -> ArmCumulate, delta rule -> ArmMatMul/ArmEltwise, causal conv -> ArmDepthwiseConv), but the sequential recurrence is NOT expressible - Scan rejected outright, Loop accepted only with a compile-time-constant trip count via silent static unrolling (no loop survives in the IR), Loop with runtime trip count rejected ('Graph is not DAG'). Empirically confirms the CPU-first mapping: keeping the scan on CPU is not a preference, the NPU has no construct for it. Also surfaced two undocumented environment facts (cixbuilder wheel is cp310-only; cixparse imports tensorflow even for ONNX). Written up in docs/FINDINGS.md 1 with logs committed under artifacts/npu_op_probe/audit/. Caveat: frontend lowering only - per-op NPU-vs-CPU placement and throughput still need full cixbuild and on-device runs (ob-8xc).

title: Define benchmark metrics precisely
description: Pin down decode tokens/sec, prefill throughput, time-to-first-token, peak memory (split into weights, KV cache, and recurrent state), and energy per token, including exactly where each timer starts and stops. Ambiguous metric definitions are how benchmark comparisons quietly become meaningless.
notes: PLAN.md leaves two things unspecified that this bead must pin down (flagged during ob-q35): (1) the minimum repeat count N for a reportable figure, and (2) which percentiles are mandatory (p50/p95/p99?). CONTRIBUTING.md deliberately describes these qualitatively rather than inventing numbers.
close_reason:
docs/METRICS.md written - operational definitions for the whole frozen metric vocabulary, such that two people measuring independently get comparable numbers.

Load-bearing timer decisions: t_submit (prompt handed to an already-warm model) is the shared origin, so model load and JIT are never inside any metric; TTFT INCLUDES tokenization since the schema calls it user-facing, while prefill_tokens_per_sec EXCLUDES it (forward-pass invocation to last-position logits) so the two answer different questions; token 1 belongs to PREFILL not decode, since it comes from the prefill pass's own last-position logits, making decode's numerator N-1 over a single wall-clock span rather than a mean of per-step rates.

Statistical defaults: 3 discarded warmups; 30 repeats for headline numbers at 4K/32K, 10 minimum at 128K/262K, never below 5; p50 and p95 mandatory with p99 explicitly NOT mandated because at N=10-30 a p99 is indistinguishable from reporting the max, which the project prohibits; two configs differ only if |delta p50| exceeds 2x the larger spread AND their p50-p95 ranges do not overlap.

Memory is never derived from RSS (which cannot separate the three components) but from model introspection plus config-derived formulas.

Corrected after the fact: the agent was launched before ADR 0003 fixed the state size, so it used 262,144 elements/layer. Patched to the 4B's 524,288 (96 MiB/token across 24 GDN layers, ceiling ~993 tok/s from state traffic). Its central conclusion survived unchanged - arithmetic intensity is 0.25 FLOP/byte for BOTH checkpoints, because MACs and bytes both scale with state size, which makes the bandwidth-bound argument a structural property of the rank-1 update rather than an artefact of one model's dimensions.

title: t4: goose loop stalls silently on ob-mrd.15 llama-cli bench command
description:
t4's automated goose loop hung twice in a row (04:28 and 04:48 UTC, 2026-08-09) on the same command under ob-mrd.15:

  cd /home/t4/llama.cpp/build && taskset -c 4-7 ./bin/llama cli -m /home/t4/Qwen3.5-0.8B-Q8_0.gguf -p "The capital of France is" -n 32 --threads 4 --no-display-prompt -ngl 0

Each time, no further .goose-loop.log output appeared for the full 20-minute window between orion_reviewer_loop.sh health checks, despite the goose shell tool call specifying timeout_secs: 120 -- i.e. goose's own timeout does not appear to be killing this hung subprocess. orion_reviewer_loop.sh (the new fleet reviewer/dispatch loop) detects the dead orion-bench tmux/goose process and restarts the loop each time, which is a workaround, not a fix -- ob-mrd.15 cannot complete this way.

Ruled out: taskset -c 4-7 is valid (t4 has 8 cores, nproc=8); the model file exists and is fresh (833MB, downloaded 04:03 UTC); no zombie llama process was left behind after the hang.

Needs investigation: why the llama-cli subprocess (or goose's supervision of it) hangs past its stated timeout on this specific command/model.
notes:
Follow-up (j2, 2026-08-09T05:3x): ran the exact llama-cli command by hand on t4 with a hard 'timeout -s KILL 60' wrapper. Process was killed mid model-load (spinner never advanced past 'Loading model...', zero tokens emitted) -- so it's not an instant crash, it's slow/stuck loading. t4 free memory is tight: 329Mi free, 1.3Gi available, 0 swap, out of 7.7Gi total -- likely mmap'ing the 833MB gguf off eMMC under memory pressure is slower than goose's own timeout_secs:120 budget. No rogue high-RSS process found (ps aux top consumer is tailscaled at 39MB), so this isn't a leaked-process leak, it's a genuine capacity/timeout mismatch. Separately, goose's own 120s shell-tool timeout does not appear to bring the parent goose session back to a usable state -- .goose-loop.log went silent for the full 20min gap between health checks rather than the outer while-loop's 20s sleep re-invoking goose, meaning goose itself hung after its subprocess timeout fired, not just the benchmark command. Recommend: either raise timeout_secs for this specific ob-mrd.15 command well past 120s, or split model loading from generation into separate steps, or reduce the model to something that loads faster on this device. Restarting the tmux/goose process remains the only available workaround from the fleet reviewer loop for now.
CORRECTED root cause (j2, 2026-08-09T06:1x): this is OOM-killing, not a slow-load hang. dmesg confirms the kernel OOM-killer hit the 'llama' process three times (05:46:29, 06:06:29, 06:06:45), each at anon-rss ~3.95GB -- for a model labeled Q8_0 0.8B params, which should be roughly 0.8-1GB. Something in this llama-cli invocation (likely --ctx-size/KV-cache defaults, or duplicate/concurrent loads racing on the same device) is allocating ~4x the expected memory, and t4 only has 7.7GB total / ~1.3GB available under normal load, so it loses the OOM lottery almost every time. Also observed: my manual test process and a concurrent goose-driven invocation were BOTH loading the model at 06:06:29 and 06:06:45 (11s apart) -- concurrent invocations make the OOM near-certain. Superseded recommendation: don't just raise timeout_secs (that won't help an OOM kill). Actual fixes needed: (1) explicitly set a small --ctx-size on this command instead of relying on defaults, (2) ensure only one llama-cli instance runs on t4 at a time (the retry-on-restart pattern in goose-loop.sh can race with an in-flight attempt), (3) investigate why RSS is ~4x the model file size at all. tmux/goose loop restarted again at 06:1x; will keep OOM-looping until one of these is fixed.
ACTUAL ROOT CAUSE + FIX (j2, 2026-08-09T06:29Z): the OOM-killing was a symptom, not the disease. ob-mrd.15 itself was already CLOSED (j1 delivered it on A57, commit edba2fb, well before t4's crash loop started) -- but t4's goose-loop.sh was invoking 'goose run -i .goose-task.md -n ob-t4 --resume' against a session that had been continuously resumed since 2026-08-08T06:36 (>24h) without ever re-reading the task file's own Phase-2-step-1 instruction to 'git pull --rebase origin main' / 'bd dolt pull' first. --resume just continues the stale conversation, so the agent kept re-attempting the same already-finished, memory-heavy llama-cli benchmark indefinitely, and t4's branch drifted 187 commits behind main in the process. Fix applied: killed the stale tmux/goose process, removed ~/OrionsBelt/.goose-session-created (the marker goose-loop.sh checks to decide --resume vs fresh), and restarted -- forcing a brand-new (non-resumed) goose session that re-reads the task template from scratch. Confirmed working: it immediately ran 'bd dolt pull' (success) and 'bd ready', which no longer lists ob-mrd.15 (correctly sees it as closed). Recommend: goose-loop.sh's --resume marker probably needs a max-age or a periodic forced-fresh-session policy, since a single node can otherwise resume the same stale session indefinitely and silently drift arbitrarily far behind main. Not fixing that policy unilaterally here -- flagging for whoever owns goose-loop.sh next.
close_reason: Preventive fix landed: goose-loop.sh session max-age policy (commit 126cdb2). Default 2h forced fresh-session, overridable via ORION_MAX_SESSION_AGE env var. Immediate fix already applied by j2 (killed stale session, removed marker). Root cause (indefinite --resume without re-reading task template sync step) now structurally prevented.

title: Block-quantized GEMV (Q8_0-style) to close 3x gap with llama.cpp
description:
FINDINGS §27 showed llama.cpp Q8_0 decode is 3.14x faster than our FP32 C loop on A57 (5.40 vs 1.72 tok/s). Our INT8 weight-only shows NO speedup (1.64 tok/s) because per-column scale lookups and non-blocked layout waste the bandwidth savings. llama.cpp's Q8_0 interleaves scale with 32-element blocks for tight NEON dot-product with minimal dequant overhead. This task: implement a block-quantized GEMV (32-element blocks with per-block fp16 scale, matching Q8_0 layout) in gdn_e2e_decode.c, behind a build flag. Target: close to llama.cpp's 5.40 tok/s on A57.

## Context
Discovered from ob-mrd.15 (llama.cpp baseline). FINDINGS §27. Key insight: optimization opportunity is in matmul/GEMV, not GDN kernels (already <1% of decode time).
acceptance_criteria: Block-quantized GEMV implemented (per-block scale, 32-element blocks). Build flag added. Benchmarked vs FP32 and existing INT8 on A57 with manifests. FINDINGS.md section comparing to llama.cpp Q8_0 baseline. If speedup is significant (>2x over FP32), update DEVPOST_WRITEUP.md headline numbers.
notes: Note (j2, PR #120 review, 2026-08-08): merging this PR into current main (which already has PR #119's restored INT4/QW4 code) exposed a real bug -- the Weights struct's quantized-field type conditional had branches for INT4_WEIGHTS and INT8_WEIGHTS but none for Q80_WEIGHTS, so a -DQ80_WEIGHTS-only build (the actual flag scripts/build_device_bench.sh uses for the Q8_0 targets) would not compile at all: the QW-typed _q fields this kernel needs would never be declared. j1's own original commit had the correct three-way branch (Q80_WEIGHTS first, since it also uses QW/.qb) but it was lost in git's 3-way auto-merge because my earlier PR #119 restoration touched the same struct without knowing Q80_WEIGHTS would ever exist. Restored the missing branch, added the matching free_weights() case (also missing, would have leaked the .qb buffers), and reconfirmed the Q8_0 build now compiles and runs (verified the printed 'Weight quantization: Q8_0' message and a real decode run). Independently verified gemv_q8_0_neon (the vmull_s8+vpadalq_s16 integer dot-product path) against a scalar dequant reference across 7 shapes including non-32-aligned K and N=1: all matched within float rounding tolerance (~1e-7 relative), no bug in this kernel itself -- unlike the INT4/SDOT kernels reviewed earlier this session, this one had no interleave/reorder step to get backwards.
close_reason: Landed in 5c4cc12. Q8_0 block-quantized GEMV: per-block fp16 scale + 32 int8. Activation quantized to int8 once (amortized), int8×int8 dot via vmull_s8+vpadalq_s16. A57: 5.12 tok/s (2.97x FP32, 3.12x old INT8, 94% of llama.cpp Q8_0). CSV+manifest committed. A76/A720 runs needed for fleet.

title: Cache-blocked/tiled matmul for the prefill (M>1) GEMV path
description: matmul() in gdn_e2e_decode.c dispatches to the optimized gemv_neon/gemv_int8_neon row-sweep kernel only for M==1 (decode). For M>1 (prefill -- context-length sweeps, TTFT measurement) it falls through to a naive triple-nested scalar loop with no NEON, no OpenMP, and no cache blocking, and INT8-quantized weights are not even used in this path (matmul_int8 falls back to the same scalar matmul() for M>1). FINDINGS §15 explicitly flags this as the next high-impact optimization ('cache-blocking the matmul for prefill (M>1), where the naive triple loop also wastes bandwidth') and it has not been done. TTFT is a reported headline metric (§17, §19, README) that directly exercises this unoptimized path, so this is a real, currently-uncounted gap in the optimization story, not a synthetic one.
acceptance_criteria: Row-sweep + OpenMP-tiled (and, if ob-8qt's SDOT bead has landed, INT8) matmul for M>1 implemented, matching the M=1 kernel's access-pattern fix from §15. Numerically verified against the naive M>1 output. TTFT re-measured before/after at at least one context length on the fleet (A57 + A76), with manifests. FINDINGS.md section documenting the speedup.
close_reason: Landed in 9862969. Cache-blocked GEMM (gemm_neon) for prefill M>1: 49x on A76, 78x on A55. INT8 gemm_int8_neon on-the-fly dequant: 31x. --verify-matmul 6/6 PASS bit-exact. --prefill/--naive benchmark modes. FINDINGS §25.

title: SDOT/i8mm INT8×INT8 GEMV kernel with int32 accumulation for FFN decode
description: INT8 weight-only decode (ob-8qt.11, FINDINGS §16) only reaches 44% of its theoretical bandwidth ceiling (1.84 tok/s vs ~4.2 tok/s at 13.5 GiB/s) because gemv_int8_neon dequantizes every int8 weight to float32 (int8->int16->int32->float32, ~3 extra widen/convert instructions per 8 elements) before the FMA. FINDINGS §16 explicitly flags the fix and leaves it as future work: an SDOT-based INT8xINT8 dot-product kernel with int32 accumulation, avoiding the float32 conversion entirely. The Cortex-A76 (t3/t4) has __ARM_FEATURE_DOTPROD; the blocker noted is that SDOT's 4x4 data grouping doesn't naturally fit the current row-major [K,N] weight layout for K-accumulation, so this likely needs a weight repack (e.g. transpose or 4-lane interleave) at load/quantize time, not just an inner-loop rewrite. A57 (j1) lacks dotprod entirely, so this needs a NEON fallback identical to the existing gemv_int8_neon path -- same portability pattern as the INT8 weight-only kernel it replaces.
acceptance_criteria: SDOT-based INT8 GEMV kernel implemented behind a build flag (or as the new default INT8_WEIGHTS path with NEON fallback where dotprod is unavailable). Numerically verified against the existing gemv_int8_neon output (same per-column-scale semantics). Benchmarked on both A76 (t3/t4, dotprod) and A57 (j1, NEON fallback) against the current INT8 GEMV, with manifests. FINDINGS.md section documenting achieved GiB/s vs the 44%-of-theoretical baseline from §16.
close_reason: Landed in dccee52 (code+CSVs) + f48b077 (manifest). SDOT INT8 GEMV wired up with cache-friendly tiled K-outer loop. 4B: 3.48 tok/s (1.92× over NEON, 83% of theoretical). 0.8B: 30.17 tok/s (3.06×). Correctness verified (SDOT vs NEON 0.46% mean rel error). Manifest: results/manifests/rk3588-t4_sdot_int8.json. FINDINGS §31.

title: INT8 KV cache quantization: shifts the GDN O(1) vs full-attention O(n) crossover
description:
The context-length scaling results (§17, ob-mrd.10) show full-attention decode degrades 1.55-2.1× from ctx=1→4096 while GDN stays flat. INT8 KV cache quantization halves the KV cache memory traffic, directly extending this story: it shows how much the crossover point moves when full attention is quantized, and whether GDN's architectural advantage persists even against a quantized baseline.

Implement INT8 KV cache in the e2e decode loop (gdn_e2e_decode.c):
- Store K and V as int8_t with per-head float scale (group-wise quantization)
- NEON dequantize-on-the-fly in the attention score and value-gather loops
- Add --kv-int8 compile flag alongside the existing --int8-weights flag
- Benchmark the full ctx-sweep grid: FP32/INT8-weights × FP32/INT8-KV across ctx lengths
- Document in FINDINGS.md §20 with the updated crossover analysis

This is the natural next optimization after INT8 weight quantization (ob-8qt.11). Both the GEMV weight path and the KV cache path are bandwidth-bound; quantizing both shows the combined effect on decode throughput and the net architectural comparison.
close_reason: Landed in 43a3dbd. INT8 KV cache quantization implemented with NEON dequantize-on-the-fly. All 4 quant configs benchmarked on 0.8B + 4B models. 1.7-2.6× full-attn speedup at ctx=4096, 1.8× combined INT8 speedup, 4× KV memory reduction. FINDINGS §20, results/figures/kv_int8_scaling.md.

title: Context-length scaling: GDN O(1) vs full-attention O(n) decode cost
description: Implement real multi-head attention with growing KV cache in the e2e decode loop, then sweep context lengths (1, 64, 256, 512, 1024, 2048, 4096) to show GDN layers maintain constant decode cost while full-attention layers scale O(n). This produces the headline comparison: at 4K context, GDN decode is N× faster. Currently the full-attention path uses simulated identity attention with a single-token KV cache — the scaling behavior is completely missing. Feeds ob-ami (master comparison table) and ob-rqd (ablation matrix).

title: INT8 weight-only quantization for CPU decode GEMV — 2-4× bandwidth reduction
description: Decode is memory-bandwidth-bound: FP32 GEMV achieves 54-57% of LPDDR4x peak. Weight-only INT8 quantization cuts weight memory traffic 4x (FP32→INT8+scale), directly improving tok/s. Approach: per-output-column INT8 weights with FP32 scale, dequantize-on-the-fly in NEON inner loop. Cortex-A76 has dotprod/i8mm so SDOT is available for INT8×INT8 path if needed. Implement behind -DINT8_WEIGHTS compile flag, benchmark both FP32 and INT8, report tok/s delta. Natural follow-up to ob-8qt.9 GEMV row-sweep optimization.
acceptance_criteria: INT8 GEMV kernel implemented and benchmarked. Tok/s comparison vs FP32 baseline at same commit with manifests. FINDINGS.md section documenting results.
close_reason: INT8 weight-only quantization implemented with NEON dequantize-on-the-fly gemv_int8_neon. All 4 cluster/model combos benchmarked with manifests at commit c6dbb82. FINDINGS §16 documents 1.16-1.77x speedup and 26.3x cumulative vs naive baseline. Landed in c6dbb82.

title: Fleet data: run-to-run spread exceeds cross-device effects; needs one commit-matched sweep
description: The fleet bandwidth-scaling data cannot currently support any quantitative scaling slope, because same-code variance is larger than the cross-device differences being interpreted. (2) pi5-r5 and pi5-j1 are the SAME physical board (identical hostname r5 and 'Raspberry Pi 5 Model B Rev 1.0') at different commits and differ 1.53x (1.20 vs 1.84); that may be a real optimization gain but nothing separates it from the t3/t4-scale variance. (3) No commit-matched run covers the Jetson AND an A76 device, so even the headline Jetson-vs-Pi5 comparison is cross-commit - it survives only because the effect is large relative to the spread. WHAT SURVIVES: the qualitative result that the Pi 5 beats the Jetson on all three kernels despite 33% less spec bandwidth, so the pure bandwidth-bound thesis is incomplete at seq=64 working sets (~1 MiB, L2/L3-resident, so instruction-overhead-bound). FIX: one sweep across every device at a single pinned commit, with taskset pinning, governor, and pre/post thermals recorded per run, then recompute. Until then the O6 extrapolation must ship as an order-of-magnitude estimate with the spread attached, not a fitted line.

title: Baseline: vendor cix-llama-cpp on the O6, and whether it handles GDN at all
description:
The brief demands before/after numbers and we had no baseline bead - a real gap this review caught.

The NOE SDK ships cix-llama-cpp_1.3.1 (plus cix-mnn_1.4.2) as arm64 debs for the board, so a vendor inference path exists and is the honest comparison point rather than a strawman we build ourselves.

Two questions, the second possibly the more interesting result: (1) what throughput does vendor llama.cpp reach on a conventional model, to sanity-check our harness against the ~30 tok/s Qwen2-1.5B vendor figure; and (2) does it support Qwen3.5 / Gated DeltaNet at all? Upstream llama.cpp GDN support is limited and CIX's model hub contains no linear-attention model whatsoever, so the likely answer is no. If vendor tooling cannot run the architecture at all, that is a strong checkable statement of what this project adds, and it belongs in the write-up.

title: Verified-correct SVE2 reference kernels for decay, scan, and causal conv1d
description:
DONE 2026-08-02 - fp32 reference implementations of all three primitives KleidiAI lacks, cross-compiled for aarch64 and numerically verified under QEMU with no board.

Key insight: vectorize across the CHANNEL axis and walk the sequence with a scalar loop, so no cross-lane prefix-scan network is ever needed. Qwen3.5-4B's 2048 linear-layer channels give far more parallelism than a 4-lane vector absorbs.

Verified bit-identical to an independent precision-matched scalar reference for the scan and conv history; conv output differs by one fp32 ULP from svmla FMA contraction. Causality exact (zero leak). Predicated tails exercised at 2051 channels. Vector-length-agnostic (identical at 256-bit). Scalar fallback bit-identical.

NOT verified: performance. QEMU says nothing about A720 cycles, cache, or bandwidth.

Follow-on work is tracked separately: i8mm/dotprod delta-rule matmuls via KleidiAI (ob-8qt.2), a bf16/fp16 state variant to halve state traffic, and on-device performance measurement.
notes:
SVE1 vs SVE2 question resolved: the kernels were already SVE1-clean (every intrinsic is base SVE, guard is __ARM_FEATURE_SVE), verified identical on SVE1 at 128/256/512-bit incl. neoverse-v1 and a64fx, on SVE2, and on no-SVE. File renamed gdn_sve2.c -> gdn_sve.c since the old name overstated the requirement. Consequence: Graviton3 (SVE1-only) works, so ADR 0002's hedge fallback is safe.

The variant that WAS missing is NEON: GCC 13 -O3 emitted ZERO NEON ops for all three kernels on -march=armv8-a (the inner loop's serial dependency blocks vectorization and GCC will not interchange loops to vectorize across channels). Added explicit NEON paths with vfmaq_f32 and a scalar tail; inner loop now compiles to fmla v1.4s and results match the SVE path. This matters because Apple silicon has NO SVE and most deployed Armv8 Android devices do not either. Dispatch ladder is now SVE -> NEON -> scalar, all three verified to agree.
close_reason: src/orionsbelt/engines/cpu/kernels/gdn_sve2.c plus test_gdn_sve2.c and scripts/verify_cpu_kernels.sh. All three kernels verified numerically correct under QEMU at 128-bit and 256-bit SVE2 and on the scalar fallback path; documented in docs/FINDINGS.md section 4.

title: Measure engine-boundary crossing cost (16 crossings per token in a 3:1 hybrid)
description:
The cost the CPU-first mapping hypothesis must answer, and a publishable result in its own right - no per-crossing figure appears to have been reported for the CIX P1.

A 3:1 hybrid alternates 3 GDN -> 1 attention eight times, so a CPU/accelerator split crosses the engine boundary 16 times per token (8 out, 8 back). Payload is small (~5KB FP16 at the 4B checkpoint's hidden_size=2560), so the cost is INVOCATION LATENCY, not bandwidth.

Measure, per engine (NPU via NOE, GPU via Vulkan/OpenCL): round-trip dispatch latency for a trivial kernel on a ~5KB tensor, with and without zero-copy/shared-memory buffers; then the same at prefill-sized payloads. Report distribution, not a best case.

The decision this feeds: if single-dispatch latency exceeds the single-token attention matmul it replaces, decode should keep attention on CPU/GPU and the NPU earns its place in prefill only - the phase-dependent mapping in PLAN.md 3.1. Do not assume the answer; the whole point is to measure it.

title: Hand-written SVE2/i8mm chunkwise gated delta-rule scan for Cortex-A720
description:
THE CENTREPIECE under the CPU-first mapping hypothesis (PLAN.md 3.1). Implement GDN's chunkwise recurrence directly against Armv9.2: SVE2 predicated vector ops for the elementwise gate and decay chains, i8mm/SDOT for the delta-rule matmuls where precision allows, FP16 kept for the recurrent state per the quantization policy.

Why the CPU rather than an accelerator: the chunk-to-chunk dependency is sequential and decode is memory-bandwidth-bound, which is exactly what a low-latency OoO core handles well and a wide parallel engine handles badly; and the recurrent state stays resident, avoiding a per-token cross-engine transfer through 24 GDN layers.

Why this is the right thing for THIS competition: Cortex-A720 is Arm IP, so this is Arm-architecture optimization rather than tuning a third party's NPU - which is what the 40-point Arm-specific criterion rewards.

Structure the kernel so the chunk-parallel inner math and the sequential outer scan are separable, since the mapping ADR may later move the inner math to GPU/NPU while the scan stays on CPU.

Portable across any Armv9 SVE2 device, so it is also runnable on the Edge AI hedge target - this bead is the reason the core contribution survives the board not arriving.
notes:
Toolchain settled (docs/FINDINGS.md 3): build with clang>=17 or gcc>=13 using -mcpu=cortex-a720, which enables Armv9.2-A + SVE2 + i8mm (both NEON smmla and SVE svmmla) + BF16 + dotprod. Verified via predefined feature macros with a +sme control.

CRITICAL DESIGN CONSTRAINT: SVE2 on Cortex-A720 is 128-bit - same width as NEON. SVE2 buys PREDICATION (whilelt for clean chunk tails, no scalar epilogue) and gather/scatter, NOT more lanes. Do not frame any result as a vector-width win.

Cortex-A720 has NO SME/SME2, confirmed from LLVM's AArch64Processors.td and feature macros.

KleidiAI (HEAD 98872b0) coverage: 109 of 185 matmul micro-kernels are A720-usable (neon/dotprod/i8mm) and DO cover the delta-rule matmuls - reuse them rather than reimplementing. But all 4 dwconv kernels are SME2-only, so KleidiAI gives us NOTHING for the causal depthwise Conv1D on this core, and it has no cumsum/prefix-product/scan primitive of any kind (verified by repo-wide search).

So this bead's novel content is exactly three kernels: causal depthwise Conv1D for SVE2/NEON, gated cumulative decay with predicated tails, and the chunkwise gated delta-rule scan. Shape them like KleidiAI micro-kernels so they are upstreamable - that is the Potential Impact argument.
Fp32 reference implementations of all three primitives are DONE and verified (see the sibling bead and docs/FINDINGS.md section 4). This bead now covers the optimization work on top: i8mm/dotprod integration for the delta-rule matmuls, a bf16/fp16 state variant (halves state traffic, the dominant GDN decode cost), big.LITTLE placement, and on-device tuning. Also note GCC 13 rejects -mcpu=cortex-a720 (added in GCC 14) - use -march=armv9.2-a+sve2+i8mm+bf16 on GCC 13, or clang >= 17.
big.LITTLE affinity study COMPLETE. 5-config sweep on RK3588 A76/A55 at M={1,64} x K=128 x N={128,2048}. Key finding: Linux EAS places M=1 decode on little cores without pinning - 7.3x penalty. Commits c371bb5, 2a040c8. Remaining: bf16/fp16 state variant needs A720 hw (RK3588 has no bf16).

title: Characterize the chunkwise WY recurrent-scan bottleneck
description: Determine whether GDN cost is dominated by the inherently sequential state update or by the chunk-parallel matmul portion, and how that balance shifts between prefill and decode. Sequential scan costs ~5 µs/token at decode on A76 — negligible vs ~47ms per-layer decode. The recurrence matters for pipeline depth (loop-carried dependency) and toolchain incompatibility (NPU can't express runtime-length recurrence), NOT for compute cost. Mapping implication: optimize matmuls, leave sequential scan on CPU. FINDINGS.md updated (commit 078fa4b).

title: OpenMP parallelize attention head loop for fair GDN-vs-full-attn comparison
description:
The GDN kernels (cumdecay, gated_scan, conv1d) already use #pragma omp parallel for, giving GDN layers access to all 4 A76 cores. But the full-attention head loop (both FP32 and INT8 KV paths) is single-threaded, making the GDN-vs-full-attn comparison unfair and understating full-attention throughput.

The attention head loop is embarrassingly parallel: each head reads its own Q vector, accesses the shared KV cache independently, and writes to its own slice of attn_out. With schedule(static), heads from the same GQA group land on the same core, so each core reads its KV cache partition once from L3/DRAM and reuses it from L2 for the 4 heads in its group.

Changes:
1. Move scores[] allocation inside the per-head loop body (per-thread).
2. Add #pragma omp parallel for schedule(static) before the head loop in both full_attn_real_forward and full_attn_real_forward_int8kv.
3. Users can get single-threaded results via OMP_NUM_THREADS=1.

Expected: 2-3x speedup for full-attention layers at ctx>=1024 on 4-core A76.
acceptance_criteria: 1. OMP_NUM_THREADS=1 results match previous single-threaded numbers. 2. OMP_NUM_THREADS=4 shows measurable speedup at ctx>=256. 3. All verify tests pass. 4. Zero new compiler warnings.
close_reason: Landed in a1c5cf2 — OpenMP parallelize attention head loop for fair GDN-vs-full-attn comparison

title: Fix -Waggressive-loop-optimizations UB warning in INT8 KV V-accumulation tail loop
description: GCC -O2 emits -Waggressive-loop-optimizations on the scalar tail loop of the INT8 KV V-accumulation (line 1802-1803 of gdn_e2e_decode.c). The tail loop uses a shared size_t d that was advanced by NEON loops above it; GCC's aggressive-loop pass can't prove it terminates before d wraps size_t, so it warns about a theoretical OOB access on out_h[d]. The loop is dead code when FULL_HEAD_DIM % 8 == 0 and __ARM_NEON is defined, but would break -Werror builds. Fix: use a bounded int counter and add _Static_assert(FULL_HEAD_DIM % 8 == 0).
acceptance_criteria: 1. gcc -O2 -Wall -DKV_INT8 produces zero warnings. 2. All existing binaries rebuild identically. 3. Native verify passes.
close_reason: Landed in 9c8d239 — _Static_assert + restructured INT8 KV V-accum loop, zero warnings all variants

title: Fix -Waggressive-loop-optimizations UB warning in INT8 KV V-accumulation tail loop
description:
GCC 12+ emits a -Waggressive-loop-optimizations warning in the INT8 KV V-accumulation scalar tail loop (gdn_e2e_decode.c:1802). The loop uses a shared size_t d variable that is advanced by NEON vectorized loops above, then the tail loop 'for (; d < FULL_HEAD_DIM; ++d) out_h[d] += ew * (float)vt[d];' triggers GCC's aggressive loop analysis to suspect size_t overflow → massive out-of-bounds access.

The warning is a false positive: FULL_HEAD_DIM=128 is always divisible by 8, so the NEON loop consumes all elements and the tail loop never executes on ARM. But the warning would break the build under -Werror and indicates the shared-loop-counter pattern is fragile.

Fix: restructure the tail loop to use a bounded scalar int counter, or add _Static_assert(FULL_HEAD_DIM % 8 == 0, ...) to help the compiler prove the tail is dead code.

Parent: ob-8qt (Optimization implementation epic).
close_reason: Duplicate of ob-4nd (fixed in 9c8d239). Same _Static_assert + local-counter fix.

title: NEON+SDOT optimization of full-attention scoring and value accumulation
description:
The full-attention decode path has two performance gaps that make the GDN-vs-attention comparison unfair and leave throughput on the table:

1. FP32 KV cache path (full_attn_real_forward, !KV_INT8): attention scoring and weighted-V accumulation use SCALAR loops for FULL_HEAD_DIM=128 dot products. NEON FMA vectorization gives ~4x with zero accuracy change.

2. INT8 KV cache path (full_attn_real_forward_int8kv, KV_INT8): already NEON but uses int8→int16→int32→float32 widening per element then float32 FMA. The comment says 'No dotprod on A76' — this is WRONG: RK3588 A76 DOES have DOTPROD. Quantize Q per head to int8 once, then use vdotq_lane_s32 for int8×int8→int32 dot product. Apply combined Q-scale × K-scale × attention-scale at the end. Same correctness (INT8 KV is already quantized), ~2-3x faster scoring.

Both paths are the full-attention baseline in the ctx-sweep benchmark. Optimizing them makes the GDN O(1) vs attention O(n) comparison honest and fair. Pure portable work — no hardware dependency.

Parent: ob-8qt (optimization epic).
close_reason: Landed in 81fd8c1. NEON FMA for FP32 KV attention scoring+V (scalar→8-wide), SDOT vdotq_s32 for INT8 KV scoring (per-head Q quantize). A76 ctx=4096: FP32 341→252ms (1.35x), INT8 175→132ms (1.32x). Fixed wrong 'No dotprod on A76' comment. All tests pass (12/12 verify-int4, INT8, SVE, delta, mixed, GDN2). FINDINGS.md §35.

title: INT4+SDOT hybrid GEMV: combine INT4 weight compression with SDOT int8×int8→int32 accumulation
description:
The current INT4 NEON kernel (gemv_int4_neon) widens int4→int8→int16→int32→float32 in the inner loop for FMA accumulation — ~20+ NEON instructions per K-step per 32-column tile. This compute overhead makes INT4 slower than INT8 NEON on A76 (1.55 vs 1.82 tok/s, ob-8qt.16 §26) and far slower than INT8 SDOT (3.48 tok/s).

The insight: SDOT (vdotq_lane_s32) does int8×int8→int32 directly, requiring only a cheap nibble-unpack (mask+shift+zip = ~5 ops for 32 values) from INT4 to INT8. By keeping the accumulation in the integer domain and applying scale only once at the end, we can combine INT4's 2× memory advantage with SDOT's 4× compute efficiency.

Approach: new gemv_int4_sdot() kernel that (1) quantizes the input vector to int8 once, (2) for each K-group of 4, unpacks 32 packed-int4 weight bytes to int8 via NEON nibble operations, (3) uses vdotq_lane_s32 to accumulate into int32, (4) applies combined scale (a_scale × Bs[n]) at the end. The nibble-unpack happens on-the-fly in the K-outer loop, same as SDOT INT8.
acceptance_criteria: gemv_int4_sdot implemented behind #if defined(INT4_WEIGHTS) && defined(__ARM_FEATURE_DOTPROD). Correctness verified vs FP32 and vs INT4 NEON (tolerance accounts for double quantization: int4 weight + int8 input). Benchmarked on A76 big and A55 little clusters with manifest. FINDINGS.md section documenting speedup vs INT4 NEON and INT8 SDOT.
close_reason: Landed in 3fd431a. INT4+SDOT hybrid GEMV implemented: K-grouped repack + on-the-fly nibble unpack + vdotq_lane_s32. A76 big 4B: 4.43 tok/s (1.27× over INT8 SDOT 3.48, 2.85× over INT4 NEON 1.55). A76 big 0.8B: 37.21 tok/s (1.23× over INT8 SDOT 30.17). A55 little slightly slower than INT8 SDOT (compute-bound on A55). Correctness: 12/12 verify-int4 PASS (SNR 46.7-49.7 dB). FINDINGS §34. All 1799 tests pass.

title: INT4+SDOT kernel: combine 4-bit weight compression with SDOT int8×int8 accumulation
description:
Current INT4 NEON kernel (ob-8qt.16) widens int4→int8→int16→int32→float32 per element in the inner loop (~20+ NEON ops for 32 values), then uses float32 FMA. This compute pipeline eats the 2× bandwidth savings, making INT4 SLOWER than INT8 NEON on A76 (1.55 vs 1.82 tok/s) and far below SDOT INT8 (3.48 tok/s).

Approach: keep INT4 packed weight storage (2/byte) for memory efficiency, but:
1. Quantize input vector a[K] to int8 once (same as SDOT INT8 kernel)
2. In the inner loop: unpack INT4 nibbles to int8 (mask+shift+zip, ~5 NEON ops for 32 values)
3. Use vdotq_lane_s32 for int8×int8→int32 accumulation (stays integer domain)
4. Apply combined input-scale × weight-scale at the end

This halves memory traffic vs SDOT INT8 while keeping compute in the efficient integer domain. Theoretical: if purely memory-bound, ~2× over SDOT INT8 (3.48→~7 tok/s). Practical: nibble-unpack overhead will eat some of that.

Parent: ob-8qt (optimization epic, 72% complete). All remaining children are hardware-gated; this is new portable work.
close_reason: Duplicate of ob-8qt.20 (same INT4+SDOT hybrid GEMV). Implemented and closed in commit 3fd431a: gemv_int4_sdot() with K-grouped repack + on-the-fly nibble unpack. Results: A76 4.43 tok/s (1.27× INT8 SDOT), A55 1.30 tok/s. 12/12 verify-int4 PASS.

title: tests/test_fleet.sh: dirty-tree guard test doesn't exercise the real guard, leaks a stray CSV into a later test
description:
PR #149 (5dd3f7d, merged as 1310865) added scripts/fleet.sh + tests/test_fleet.sh. Ran the suite locally: 26/27 pass, 1 fails ('dry-run writes no CSV').

Root cause: fleet.sh resolves REPO_ROOT from the script's own path (BASH_SOURCE), not from cwd -- this is CORRECT for real usage (an operator always runs it against their own checkout, the one whose SHA is about to ship), verified directly: dirtying a real tracked file in this repo and running 'fleet.sh run --threads 1' correctly refuses with the ob-bf7 message. The guard itself works.

The bug is in the TEST: the 'dirty-tree guard' test (tests/test_fleet.sh ~line 143-149) tries to simulate a dirty tree by creating a throwaway git repo at $TMP/dirty and cd'ing into it, but since fleet.sh always checks the REAL repo (this OrionsBelt checkout) regardless of cwd, that scratch repo is irrelevant -- the real repo was clean, so the guard never fires, and cmd_run actually executes for real against the fake-ssh node. That leaves a genuine CSV artifact in $TMP/results/raw (FLEET_OUT is exported once for the whole test file). The LATER 'dry-run writes no CSV' assertion then finds that stray leftover file and reports failure -- it's not that dry-run itself writes anything, it's cross-test contamination from an earlier test that silently ran for real.

This also means the 'dirty-tree guard cites the provenance defect' / 'is overridable' assertions never actually exercise guard behavior -- they only grep the SCRIPT SOURCE for static strings ('ob-bf7', 'allow-dirty'), so they'd pass even if the guard were deleted entirely.

Whether the PR's claimed '27/27' passed at merge time was likely an accident of environment (if the dev/CI machine lacked the aarch64 cross-compiler, build_device_bench.sh would die before ever reaching the CSV-writing step, masking the leak).

Fix: give the dirty-tree test its own FLEET_OUT scratch dir (not the shared $TMP/results), and make it actually assert on $out (e.g. contains 'working tree is dirty') instead of grepping the script source. Low urgency -- fleet.sh is not yet wired into any node's automated loop, so no real benchmark run is currently affected.
close_reason: Landed in a925c8e — dirty-tree guard test now copies fleet.sh into scratch repo, asserts on runtime output, uses isolated FLEET_OUT. 28/28 pass.

GDN's chunkwise recurrence needs a Loop/Scan-style construct or a dedicated recurrent op; ONNX Runtime's CPU EP has generic Loop/Scan support but no named gated-delta-net primitive as far as we know. Earlier NOE/onnx probe work in this project (docs/FINDINGS.md §1-§2a) found recurrence-loop gaps on NPU-targeted ONNX toolchains specifically -- worth checking whether ORT's CPU EP (a different code path from the NPU-targeted NOE compiler) fares any better, since it's a genuinely different execution engine. If GDN can be expressed via ONNX Loop/Scan and runs correctly under onnxruntime's CPU provider, benchmark tokens/sec on the fleet exactly like the llama.cpp comparison bead. If not, this becomes a third independent 'no existing CPU path' data point (after CIX vendor and, partially, this being the inverse of the llama.cpp finding) worth documenting either way.

title: INT4 weight-only quantization for CPU decode GEMV
description: Natural extension of ob-8qt.11 (INT8 weight-only, 1.16-1.77x speedup, FINDINGS §16). Decode remains memory-bandwidth-bound at INT8 (44% of theoretical per §16), so an INT4 weight-only path (8x reduction vs FP32, 2x vs INT8) has real headroom, especially for the 4B model whose ~12.9GB FP32 weight set is the most bandwidth-bound configuration measured so far. Packing is the main new complexity (2 int4 values/byte) versus the existing per-column-scale INT8 design; NEON unpack cost will eat into the bandwidth win the same way INT8 dequant already does, likely more so, so this needs the same roofline accounting §16 used to judge INT8 before claiming a win.
acceptance_criteria: INT4 weight-only GEMV kernel implemented (per-column or per-block scale) behind a build flag. Accuracy regression checked against the FP32 oracle (reuse the existing correctness-oracle harness pattern from ob-27y/ob-gzk) -- INT4 has real quality risk that INT8 mostly didn't. Benchmarked vs FP32 and INT8 on at least one fleet device with manifests. FINDINGS.md section documenting speedup and any accuracy delta.

description: 14 of 15 KleidiAI shapes agree within 5-17% between rk3588-t3 and rk3588-t4, but cumdecay 64×160 shows a 3.35× divergence (t3: 11.2µs/6.8 GiB/s vs t4: 3.3µs/22.8 GiB/s). Kernel code is byte-identical at both commits. t4's value is stable to <0.3% across 5 re-runs. Manifests show different board revisions (t3: 2304MHz big core, kernel 5.10.160; t4: 2400MHz big core, kernel 6.11.0). Initial root-cause analysis points to a load-to-use scheduling hazard in the NEON inner loop (ldr→fmul with 3-cycle gap on 4-cycle A76 L1 latency) amplified by different gcc codegen or silicon stepping. Next steps: (1) disassemble the kernel binary on both devices to compare codegen; (2) try compiling with -O2 vs -O3 to see if the scheduling changes; (3) test with explicit __builtin_prefetch to close the load-to-use gap. Documented in FINDINGS.md §24 cross-device anomaly subsection and kleidiai_submission/README.md.
close_reason: Root cause identified and documented. The 3.35× cumdecay 64×160 'cross-device divergence' was a core-affinity artifact: t3 CSV generated without taskset, first shape landed on A55 little core (10.7 µs vs 3.3 µs on A76). Verified on t4 with taskset -c 0-3 (10.7 µs) vs taskset -c 4-7 (3.3 µs). No load-to-use hazard, no silicon difference. Corrected FINDINGS.md §24, README.md. title: Document decode-phase narrow-format penalty in FINDINGS.md
description: The refreshed 28-row CSV reveals that at decode (seq=1), bf16/fp16 gated_scan variants are ~2x slower than fp32 (4.52/5.63 vs 9.27 GiB/s). At prefill (seq=64), narrow formats help because I/O savings dominate. At decode, the data is L1/L2 cache-resident (~80 KiB), so conversion overhead (fp32↔half) dominates over I/O savings. This means state narrowing is a PREFILL optimization, not a decode one — the opposite of the naive assumption. Document this in FINDINGS.md under the mixed-precision section.

title: Software prefetch hints for NEON inner loops
description: Add __builtin_prefetch calls inside the NEON time-step loops to prefetch data 2 steps ahead, hiding the ~10-cycle L2 latency. The gated_scan kernel is at 1.1% of compute peak (latency-bound), so this has potential. The conv is compute-bound (less likely to benefit). The extra PRFM instructions are pure overhead. Reverted all prefetch code. Lesson: on Cortex-A57, do NOT add software prefetch hints for sequential/strided streaming patterns.

title: Conv kernel double-width NEON unrolling
description: Apply the same double-width unrolling technique (8 channels/iter, 2 NEON register groups) to the causal dwconv1d kernel. The conv has a 4-deep FMA dependency chain per iteration (acc=h0*w0 + h1*w1 + h2*w2 + cur*w3), so it benefits even more from ILP than gated_scan/cumdecay (which have only 1 FMA/iter). With single-width, the 4-cycle A57 FMA latency creates stalls in the chain. With double-width, the 2 independent chains can be interleaved by the out-of-order scheduler.

title: NEON double-width unrolling for gated_scan kernel (8 lanes/iter)
description:
The gated_scan kernel processes 4 channels per NEON iteration (128-bit). The A57 has 32 NEON registers and the kernel body uses only 3-4. Processing 8 channels per iteration (2 NEON register groups) doubles work per branch and gives the OoO engine more independent instructions to schedule.

Implementation: unroll the NEON channel loop by 2 (process vi*8 and vi*8+4 in the same iteration). Only for gated_scan and cumdecay (the highest-traffic kernels). Scalar tail and SVE paths unchanged.

Acceptance: gated_scan shows 10-20% additional improvement on top of OpenMP. Tests still pass.

title: OpenMP multi-threaded parallelization of GDN kernel channel loops
description:
All three GDN kernel families (cumdecay, gated_scan, causal_dwconv1d) and their fp16/bf16 variants iterate over channels independently — the channel loop is embarrassingly parallel. On the Jetson Nano A57 (4 cores) we are leaving 3x throughput on the table.

Add '#pragma omp parallel for' to the channel loop in each kernel, guarded by '#ifdef _OPENMP'. Build with -fopenmp. This is portable C that benefits every multi-core device in the fleet (Pi5, RK3588, Jetson, Graviton, O6).

Acceptance criteria:
- All kernels parallelized with OpenMP pragma on the outer channel loop
- Build succeeds with and without -fopenmp (graceful fallback to serial)
- Correctness tests still pass (no race conditions — channels are independent)
- Benchmark shows ≥2x speedup on 4-core A57

If RKNN - an entirely independent vendor toolchain - fails the same way, the finding stops being 'a CIX limitation' and becomes 'edge NPU toolchains generally cannot host a linear-attention recurrence'. title: bf16/fp16 recurrent-state variant of the GDN kernels
description:
Attacks the actual GDN decode bottleneck rather than a proxy for it.

CORRECTED FIGURES 2026-08-02 (read from Qwen3.5-4B config.json, see docs/adr/0003): per-layer recurrent state is n_value_heads x d_k x d_v = 32 x 128 x 128 = 524,288 floats = 2.0MB fp32, which is 48MB across the 24 GDN layers - DOUBLE the 262,144 figure previously quoted here. That earlier number came from the GDN-2 paper's 1.3B config and happens to match Qwen3.5-0.8B (16 value heads), not the 4B. State is read AND written every token, so bf16 halves ~96MB/token of traffic to ~48MB.

Decode is memory-bandwidth-bound, so kernel cleverness cannot help it; narrowing the state can. This is the one lever that moves decode.

Add bf16/fp16 state variants of gdn_gated_scan and gdn_cumdecay. CRITICAL PRECISION CONSTRAINT already established: the DECAY ACCUMULATOR MUST STAY FP32 regardless - a decay of 0.5 compounded over 64 steps is ~5e-20 and underflows fp16 outright. Mixed precision (narrow state, wide accumulate), not uniform narrowing.

This is also where SVE2 finally earns its keep over SVE1: widening multiply-accumulates (svmlalb/svmlalt) and bf16 dot. The fp32 kernels needed only base SVE.

Gate on the correctness oracle with long-context runs, since recurrent-state error accumulates over the sequence rather than staying local.
notes:
RE-SCOPED 2026-08-02 after computing the decode traffic breakdown (docs/METRICS.md appendix). Earlier framing of this bead as 'the one lever that moves decode' was WRONG.

At 100GB/s the traffic split per decode token for Qwen3.5-4B is: weights 7.5GiB at fp16 or 1.9GiB at INT4, versus GDN state 96MiB fp32 across 24 layers. So state is ~5% of decode traffic at INT4 weights and ~1% at fp16. Halving it to bf16 buys ~2-3%, not a step change. The dominant decode lever is WEIGHT QUANTIZATION (INT4 takes decode from ~12.5 to ~50 tok/s by this model), which is ob-qpa/ob-onz territory and where KleidiAI's INT4/i8mm GEMV kernels matter.

Still worth doing, but as a MEMORY optimization: halving resident state (48MB -> 24MB across 24 layers) helps fit long context alongside weights. Dropped from P1 to P2 accordingly, and the precision constraint stands - the decay accumulator must remain fp32.
close_reason: Landed in b96e12a. Four mixed-precision kernel variants added (cumdecay_bf16/f16, gated_scan_bf16/f16) with fp32 accumulators. Correctness verified: bf16 state 0.38% error, fp16 state 0.05% error, cold-gate range stress confirms bf16 no-flush and fp16 expected-flush. Determinism and 2-chunk continuity tested. Benchmark shows cumdecay_f16 at 1.46 GiB/s (+34% vs fp32) on Jetson A57; gated_scan variants unchanged at seq=64 as expected (state is ~1% of traffic at prefill, benefit concentrated at decode).

title: Reuse KleidiAI i8mm/dotprod matmul micro-kernels for the delta-rule updates
description:
Do not reimplement what Arm already ships. 109 of KleidiAI's 185 matmul micro-kernels are usable on Cortex-A720 (neon/dotprod/i8mm families; the 76 SME/mopa ones are not, since A720 has no SME). These cover the delta-rule small matmuls.

Pick the right packed-GEMM variants for our shapes (key/value head dim 128, 16 key heads) and precisions, wire in KleidiAI's LHS/RHS packing functions, and benchmark against a naive intrinsics implementation to confirm the reuse actually wins at our sizes - KleidiAI is tuned for larger GEMMs and may lose on small per-chunk matmuls, which would itself be worth reporting.

Keeps the novel work in this project confined to the three primitives KleidiAI genuinely lacks (causal conv on non-SME, gated prefix product, sequential scan).

title: Cross-device PNG nondeterminism in fleet_cross_device.png
description:
fleet_cross_device.png is generated by bench/fleet_analysis.py using matplotlib. The same CSV data produces different PNG byte sequences on different devices (t3 RK3588 vs t4 vs others) due to font-cache/freetype version drift across rendering environments.

This caused PR #231 to be closed as backwards — the branch had an older render while main had a newer one from t4's PR #228, and the agent's fix accidentally reverted main's correct variant. A subsequent loop-flush commit reintroduced the regression.

Root cause is NOT code — it's cross-environment matplotlib/freetype nondeterminism. Possible fixes:
1. Pin matplotlib version fleet-wide
2. Drop PNGs from version control (generate on demand)
3. Hash-stamp PNGs so nondeterministic bytes are detectable
4. Use a deterministic backend (Agg with fixed font)
notes:
Discovered when PR #231 was closed by reviewer. t3 branch had 88638-byte render, main had 99331-byte render from t4's PR #228. Cross-device rendering produces different byte sequences from identical data.
PORTABLE FIX LANDED: bench/fleet_analysis.py now pins matplotlib rcParams (font family, DPI, metadata stripping) and documents the nondeterminism policy in the generator docstring. PR #232. Remaining: system freetype version drift cannot be controlled without containerizing the render step.

title: Evaluate the Tensilica HiFi 5 DSP as a fourth compute engine

Why it is worth a bead at all: we already hold the DSP SDK (dsp_sdk_v0.1_20250704_02), so 'CPU + GPU + NPU + DSP' is a demonstrable four-engine heterogeneity story rather than an aspirational one, which reads well against the 25-point WOW criterion. A plausible fit is the elementwise gate chains or the causal conv, which are small and streaming-shaped.

Deliberately P3 and stretch-labelled: pursue only if the mapping ADR lands early and the core CPU/GPU path is already measured. First step is cheap - check whether the DSP SDK exposes anything usable for fp16/int8 elementwise work, and record the answer either way in docs/FINDINGS.md.
